title: Chapter 50: The Roof Garden, Part 4 of 5: The Woman in Gray
html:
She was kneeling at the end of the long bed, where the path turned, half hidden from him by the corner of a box hedge. That was why he had not seen her.
He moved. Only a little. One step along the landing, crutch and good foot, to the next gap in the railings. And then he could see her.
She was a woman of perhaps fifty, kneeling on a small square cushion of gray leather on the gravel, the kind of cushion that gardeners kneel on. She was dressed all in gray. A plain gray dress of soft wool, long, with a high neck and long sleeves, and over it a gray apron with a deep pocket in the front, and over her shoulders a gray knitted shawl, crossed over her breast and tied behind. On her hands she wore gardening gloves of gray leather, a little too big for her, the fingers soft and creased and stained dark at the tips with earth. Her hair was dark, and going gray at the front in two soft wings, and it was put up simply at the back of her head, with no ornament in it at all, and a few strands had come loose and hung down by her cheek. She did not push them back.
Beside her on the gravel there was a flat wooden basket, like a basket for eggs, and in the basket there were bulbs. Brown papery bulbs, round, each the size of a small onion, laid in rows.
She was planting them.
Corin watched her do it.
She took a bulb out of the basket. She turned it over in her gloved fingers, once, looking at it, to find which end was the top. Then she made a hole in the black earth with a small trowel, a short sharp steel trowel with a handle of pale wood. The ground was frozen on top, and the trowel scraped, and she had to lean on it to get it in. She did not hurry. She made the hole, and she put the bulb in it, top end up. And she pushed the earth back over it with the side of her gloved hand. And she patted it. Twice. Gently. The way you would pat a child's back to help it sleep. And there was a little mound, the same size as every other little mound in the bed. And she moved her cushion along the gravel one hand's width, and took another bulb out of the basket.
She did it again.
And again.
Her face was very calm.
That was what Corin would remember most, afterward, when he tried to write it down. Not how she looked. How calm she was. It was a good face, a kind face, not beautiful but pleasant, with a wide brow and soft eyes and a mouth that looked as if it had once laughed a great deal. And it was perfectly, perfectly calm. Not peaceful. Peaceful was something you got to, after something else. Peaceful was a road with an end. This was not that. This was calm the way a pond is calm when there is no wind, and no fish, and nothing under the water at all. It was calm all the way down.
Corin had seen faces like that before.
He had seen them all autumn. In the long gray rooms of the Ministry, where the Slates sat at their desks and copied and did not look up. On Felix, in Warden Briggs's line, smiling at nothing. On old Terrence, Juno's grandfather, in his chair by Marta's range among all those stopped clocks, rubbing his thumb on a key that was not there. On the children in the crypt, on their pallets, with their eyes open.
She was a Slate.
She was a Slate, on her knees in a garden on the roof of the Archon's palace, planting bulbs in the frost.
She made another hole. The trowel went in, and stopped, and she leaned on it, and it went in a little further, and then it stopped again, against something. She took the trowel out. She looked into the hole. And then she put two gloved fingers down into the black earth and brought something up.
It was a bulb.
A brown papery bulb, the same as the ones in her basket. Already planted. It had been in the ground a while. A few days, perhaps, or a week. It had a little pale root coming out of the bottom of it, like a white thread.
She looked at it.
Corin held his breath.
She turned it over in her fingers, once, the way she had turned the others. She looked at the little white root. Her calm face did not change at all. Then she put the bulb back in the hole. Gently. Top end up. And she took a new bulb out of her basket and put that in the hole too, on top of the first one. And pushed the earth back over both of them with the side of her hand. And patted it, twice.
And moved her cushion along one hand's width, and took another bulb.
Corin looked at the bed.
At the rows and rows of little mounds, all exactly the same size, a hand's width apart, all the way along the bed. At the next bed, which had mounds in it too. And the next. He did not know how deep the earth was on that roof. He did not know how many bulbs could be put into one hole, one on top of another, before the hole was full. He thought that nothing in that bed would come up in the spring. He thought that nothing in that bed had come up for a very long time.
And then the woman in gray began to hum.
She did it very softly, under her breath, the way people hum when they are working with their hands and do not know they are doing it. The way Mrs. Doyle hummed by the braziers. The way Gideon hummed his father's carrying tune in his sleep. A small low sound, not meant for anybody.
Three notes.
Corin knew them.
He knew them before he knew that he knew them, the way he had known the peppermint in the carriage window. They went into him like a hook.
He had heard them in the autumn. On his first morning in the Ink Quarter, the morning of the dead scribe, from a busker on a corner with a cracked fiddle and a dog asleep at his feet. He had heard them again that night, in the jar. When he had taken the scribe's Ash and sealed it, and held the jar up to the lamp in his room on Tallow Street, the soft gray light inside the glass had moved, and turned, and hummed. Three notes. Pell Dorran's last minutes, humming a song. He had written it down in the Ledger. The Ash hums. Three notes. I don't know the song. And he had heard them again since. From a girl in a white coat, Wren Halloway, at her desk in the Long Office, without knowing she was doing it. She hums three notes while she copies, Rowan had said. The whole Long Office stopped to listen. I knew them. The first three. Lyra had told him that on Thursday. And on Friday night, last night, on the floor of the vault, in her mother's gown, she had said it again. It's hers. Isn't it. Mother's.
Three notes. The beginning of a song. Every time, the same three notes, going up, and then stopping. As if that was all of it there was. As if the song had been cut off there, with a knife, and nobody had the rest.
The woman in gray hummed the three notes.
And then she went on.
She went on past them. Into the fourth note, and the fifth. Softly, in her low calm voice, not singing, only humming, while her gloved hands made a hole in the frozen earth and put a bulb in it. The tune went on. It went up. It climbed, slowly, step by step, the way Corin had climbed the stair. And then at the top it stopped climbing, and hung there. One long note, held, very soft, at the top of everything. Hanging. Like a moon on a string.
And then it came down.
Slowly. Gently. Note by note, the way a leaf comes down from a tree on a still day, turning. All the way down, to where it had started. And stopped. And was quiet.
And she patted the earth over the bulb. Twice.
Corin stood at the railings with his black hand round a cold iron bar and did not move.
He did not know what was happening to him. He did not know what he felt. It was not a memory. He knew what memories felt like. He had spent his whole life with them, taking them out of the dead, putting them in jars, burning his own to light his hands. A memory had a shape. It had a place, and a time, and a face in it. This had no shape. It was just a feeling, very deep in his chest, under the breastbone. A feeling like a door in a dark house that you have walked past every day of your life, and never noticed, and suddenly, one day, it is open a crack, and there is light coming out of it.
She moved her cushion along. She took another bulb.
And she hummed it again. From the beginning. The three notes, and then the rest. Up, and up, and the long note at the top, hanging. And down.
This time, at the top, on the long note, she sang.
Not loudly. Hardly at all. So softly that Corin was not sure, afterward, that he had heard words at all, and not just the shape of words, the way you hear words in the wind. But he thought he heard them. Three of them. Four. Sung on the long hanging note, in that low calm voice, to nobody, to the frozen earth.
—and let her go—
And then the tune came down again, without words, to the bottom. And stopped.
The woman in gray patted the earth. Twice.
Corin found that he was holding the iron railing with both hands. He did not remember letting go of the crutch. It was leaning against the wall beside him, and he was holding the railing with both black hands, so hard that the cold iron hurt, and his forehead was nearly touching the bars.
He made himself let go with one hand. He made himself pick up the crutch.
Who are you? he thought.
She did not look up. She had not looked up once. She did not know he was there. He was a coal man on a public stair, behind a railing, in the cold, and she was a woman in a garden, planting bulbs that would never come up, humming a song that nobody else in the city knew the end of.
Except one, Corin thought. A boy of sixteen in a cadet's coat, who had stood in a bell tower on Thursday and told his sister that he had lain awake in the dark and heard the rest of it in his head. Going down and round and home. Lyra had told Corin that, word for word, the way she told him everything now.
Rowan had the rest of it, somewhere, in the dark.
And so did she.
Inside him, in the room behind the door, the held breath went on being held. Malakor did not move. Malakor did not speak. But Corin could feel him there now, very clearly, for the first time in six days. Not gone. Not out. Pressed up against the inside of Corin's head the way a man presses himself flat against a wall in the dark when someone walks past with a lamp.
And then, behind the woman in gray, at the far end of the garden, the tall glass doors into the palace opened.
Two men came out onto the gravel.
Peppermint
Corin knew them both.
The first one out was Pallister. He came through the tall glass doors and down onto the gravel with his ebony stick, slowly, favoring his left knee, the way he had come down the steps of the stage at the Fish Stairs. He had taken off his gray coat with the fur collar. Underneath it he wore a plain dark suit, very well made, and a gray silk waistcoat with a gold chain across it, and his white thistledown hair stood up round his pink scalp in the cold air. He had the little silver box in his left hand. He was still smiling.
The second one out stopped in the doorway.
He stopped, and looked back at the glass doors, and at the handle of the one he had just come through, and put out his hand and touched the handle, once, as if to be sure it was there. Then he came out onto the gravel too.
He was young. About twenty-five. Thin, not like Silas, not like a heron, but like a pen. Narrow and straight and very neat from the top of his head to the soles of his shoes. His hair was black and cut very short and combed flat with something that made it shine, even on a gray day. He wore a long black coat, a deep and perfect black, buttoned to the throat, and on the left breast of it, small, in silver thread, there was an open book and a closed eye, and above the eye a tiny silver crown. Under one arm he had a leather folder tied with black ribbon. In his other hand he held a slim tall black book with a silver clasp, flat against his chest, with his fingers spread over it, the way some people hold a prayer book in church.
Corin had seen him once before. In the autumn. In the Second Basement of the Ministry, in Toby's office, at the ninth bell exactly, after three small quick knocks on an iron door and then three more.
My name is Lucian. I am secretary to his Excellency the Archon.
Corin pressed himself back from the railings, just a little. Into the shadow of the corner of the wall. He did not think they could see him. He was on a dark stair, behind black iron bars, under a gray sky, with a black face. But Lucian's large dark anxious eyes were already going round the garden, fast, the way they had gone round Toby's office. The paths. The hedges. The pool. The beds. The woman on her knees. The wall. The railings. They went along the railings, and over the gap where Corin stood, and did not stop, and went on.
Corin let out his breath.
Pallister had gone along the path to the end of the long bed, to where the woman in gray was kneeling. He stopped there, leaning on his stick, and looked down at her, and his round pink face went soft with kindness.
"Good afternoon, my lady," he said.
His voice carried very clearly in the cold still air. It was a pleasant voice, light and warm, a little high, the voice of a man who has spent his life saying kind things to children.
The woman stopped humming. She looked up. Her calm face did not change.
"Good afternoon," she said.
"And how is the bed today?"
"Very well, thank you." She looked down at the black earth, at the rows of little mounds. "I am putting them in for the spring."
"Just so," said Pallister warmly. "Just so. It will be very fine in the spring." He opened the little silver box with his thumb. "A peppermint, my lady? To keep out the cold?"
She looked at the box.
Then she took off one gray glove, the right, slowly, finger by finger. Her hand underneath was white and slim, and very clean, and there was a ring on it, a plain band, on the third finger. She put two fingers into the silver box and took out a small white sweet.
"Thank you," she said.
She did not eat it. She put it into the pocket of her apron. The deep pocket in the front. And as she did it the pocket moved, and sagged, and Corin saw that it was heavy. That it was full. That there were dozens of little white sweets in there already, perhaps a hundred, a whole pocketful of them, rattling softly together like pebbles as she put the new one in among them.
She did not eat them. She never ate them. Like Kitty Kane, with her jar at home. She did not know why.
She put her glove back on, finger by finger. And bent over the bed again, and took a bulb from the basket.
Pallister closed his silver box with a little click, and stood a moment longer looking down at her, smiling. Then he turned, and came back along the path toward the frozen pool, where Lucian was waiting.
They stopped by the pool.
They stopped not ten paces from the railings. From the corner of the wall. From Corin.
He did not breathe.
"Four minutes," said Lucian.
His voice was just as Corin remembered it. Soft and quick and precise, every word set down separately, like coins counted onto a table.
"His Excellency has the Council papers until the quarter. Then he will see you. Until the quarter past. I have it written." He opened the black book with its silver clasp and looked at a page. He closed it. He opened it again and looked at the same page. He closed it. "I have it written."
"Of course, my dear boy, of course." Pallister leaned on his stick and looked out over the low wall at the city below, the whole gray smoking spread of it going down to the river. He breathed in, as if the cold air were good wine. "What a view. I never tire of it. Every Saturday, Lucian, I say to myself, there it is. All of it. Every chimney." He smiled. "Every child."
Lucian's mouth pressed itself together.
"The Saint Bride's notice," he said.
"Ah. Yes."
"His Excellency has seen it. He approves." Lucian looked at his book. "He asks only that it be done before the bells. Quietly. Without—" He looked at the book again. "Without distress. To the parish."
"There is never distress, Lucian." Pallister sounded almost hurt. "There are sweets."
"Yes."
"Fifty-one. One fewer than we hoped. There was a boy on Monday who went before we could fetch him. A pity. But fifty-one is a good number. And the others, the ones on the other church doors, the general notice, we shall see. We shall see what Midwinter brings." Pallister turned the silver box over in his gray-gloved fingers. "The carts are ready. Six of them. Blankets in every one. Hot bricks for their feet. I have seen to it myself."
"And the doctor," said Lucian.
Pallister sighed.
"Poor Silas," he said. "A good man. A tired man. Four letters, Lucian. Four. Each one longer than the last. I have them on my desk. I read them, you know. I read every word." He shook his white head. "He cares so very much. That is always the trouble with the good ones. They care so much that they cannot see what is kind."
"The Inquisition will collect him," said Lucian. "On Sunday. In the evening. At the Inquisitor's own request." He looked at the book. "His Excellency asks that you not be present."
"I never am," said Pallister gently.
Corin stood in the corner of the wall with his black hand round the iron bar and felt the cold go into him, all the way into the bone.
Sunday. In the evening.
Tomorrow.
"There is one small thing more," said Pallister, after a moment. He said it lightly, looking at the view. "A very small thing. You will think it silly. There was a matter at the Lady's house, last Sunday. In the cellar. One of my bags was opened. One vial went missing. Nineteen, where there should be twenty, and a hole in the straw." He turned the silver box over again. "And a twist of sweets. And a letter of the doctor's, from my own bag, that I had written on. It troubles me, Lucian. Not the vial. I have a great many vials. It is the letter. I wrote on it. Keep him busy. I would not want anybody to read that who did not understand it."
Lucian opened his book. He looked at a page for a long time. He closed it.
"His Excellency knows," he said.
Pallister stopped turning the box.
"Does he?"
"He knows." Lucian's long pale fingers were spread flat over the black cover. "He asked me to tell you. If you raised it. He said—" He opened the book again. He read from it, very carefully, word by word, as if he were reading out a sentence in a court. "Tell Ambrose that it does not matter what is lost. It only matters what is remembered. And by whom."
There was a little silence by the frozen pool.
Pallister's round pink face did not change. He was still smiling. But the smile had gone very still, the way a clock goes still when it stops, with its hands still pointing at the same hour.
"How wise," he said softly. "How very like him."
And then, from the end of the long bed, where the woman in gray was kneeling with her trowel in the frozen earth, the humming started again. The three notes. And then the rest. Going up, and up, and hanging.
Lucian's head turned toward it, sharply.
He looked at her for a moment. His mouth pressed itself together so hard that it went white. Then he looked down at his book, and opened it, and did not read it.
"She hums that," he said. "Every week. When she is in the garden."
"Charming," said Pallister. He had begun to smile properly again. "It's an old tune, isn't it? I used to hear the river people sing it. Long ago. Before the war. Something about a fisherman." He put his head on one side, listening, like a bird. "I've forgotten how it goes."
"His Excellency does not mind it," said Lucian.
He said it quickly, the way a man says something he has been told to say.
Pallister looked at him. And then he laughed, very softly, a little pink pleased laugh, and patted the young man on the arm with his gray glove.
"You work too hard, Lucian," he said. "You always have. All those stairs. All those books. Here." He held out the silver box, open. "Have a sweet."
Lucian looked at the box.
For a moment, perhaps two breaths, he did not move at all. He stood very straight by the frozen pool, with the leather folder under his arm and the black book against his chest, and looked down at the little white sweets in their silver box. And his large dark anxious eyes went very wide.
"No," he said. "Thank you. No."
He took one step back. One tiny step, to his left, away from the box, the way he had stepped away from the jars on Toby's shelves in the autumn.
"I don't take sweets," said Lucian. "I never take sweets. I have it—" He stopped.
Pallister closed the box. Click.
"Just so," he said pleasantly. "Just so."
Somewhere inside the palace, deep in the white walls, a clock began to strike. Not a bell. A clock. A small sweet silver chime, very far away, like a spoon on a glass. One. Two. Three. And then a pause. And then a fourth.
The quarter.
Lucian's head came up.
"The quarter," he said. He opened his book. He looked at it. He closed it. He opened it again. "The quarter. His Excellency." He turned toward the glass doors. "This way, please, Under-Secretary. This way. Mind the step. There is a step."
"I know there is a step, dear boy. I come every week."
"Yes. There is a step."
They went back along the gravel. Pallister first, slowly, with his stick, favoring his left knee. Lucian behind, with his book. At the glass doors Lucian stopped, and held one of them open, and Pallister went in. And then Lucian looked back. Once. Over his shoulder. At the garden. At the paths and the hedges and the frozen pool and the woman in gray on her knees at the end of the long bed, humming.
At the railings.
His eyes went along them again. Fast. The way they had before. And this time, at the gap in the corner, where Corin stood pressed back into the shadow with his black face and his black hands, they stopped.
They stopped for perhaps one breath.
Then Lucian went in, and pulled the glass door shut behind him, and Corin saw his narrow black shape through the glass put out a hand and touch the handle, once, to be sure it was shut. And then he was gone.
The Voice
Then it was just the two of them again. The woman in the garden, and the man on the stair.
She did not know he was there. He knew that. But it felt, for a while, as if they were alone together on the top of the world, the two of them, with the whole gray city lying below them like a sleeping animal, and the low clouds over it, and the spire going up into the clouds behind the dome. The wind had dropped. It was very still. Somewhere far below, down the slope of the Hill, a dog was barking, and the sound came up thin and small, as if from the bottom of a well. And from the back gate, round the curve of the wall, he could just hear, every little while, the long roaring rattle of coal going down the chute. Abner. Sack after sack. Juno pulling them to the edge.
He should go back down. He knew that. He had seen what he came to see. He had heard more than he came to hear. Sunday. In the evening. He should go down the forty-four steps, sideways, with the bad leg going first, and get back on the cart, and go back to the crypt, and tell Silas that the Inquisition was coming for him tomorrow night. That was what mattered. That was the thing that could still be changed.
He did not go.
He stood at the railing and watched her plant bulbs.
She went on with it the same as before. As if the two men had never come out. As if nobody had ever offered her a sweet. The trowel into the frozen earth, scraping. The bulb out of the basket, turned over once, top end up. Into the hole. The earth pushed back with the side of her gloved hand. Two pats. And move the cushion along, one hand's width. And she hummed. The three notes, and then the rest. Up, and up, and hanging. And down.
Corin found that he was learning it.
He did not mean to. He could not sing. He had never been able to sing, as far as he knew, and he had never had anybody tell him otherwise. But he found that he could hear the tune coming before it came. The fourth note, after the three. The fifth. The climb. He knew, now, when the long note at the top was coming, and how long she would hold it, and which way the first note would fall when it came down. He did not know how he knew. He had heard it four times. Five. That was not enough to learn a tune. It was not enough for anybody.
It was as if he were not learning it at all. As if he were remembering it.
He pushed that thought away. It was not true. He did not have it. He had looked, all autumn, every time the three notes came, in Pell's jar, in the busker's fiddle, in Wren's humming. He had looked inside himself for the rest of it, in all the dark empty rooms where his memories used to be, and it had never been there. Not once. It was not his. It was hers. Lyra's mother's. Rowan's, in the dark. This woman's, in her garden.
She began it again. The three notes. The climb.
And she had got almost to the top, almost to the long hanging note, when the glass doors at the end of the garden opened.
Only one of them. Only a little. A hand's width, the way the carriage window had been open on the Crescent. And there was nobody on the gravel. Nobody came out. Corin could see, through the misted glass of the door, a tall shape standing just inside it, in the warm, a dark shape against the light of the room behind. That was all. A shape. And the edge of a sleeve at the gap in the door. Gray. Pale gray, like a dove's wing. And the fingers of a hand resting on the edge of the glass door, holding it open. A long hand, in a pale gray glove.
And a voice came out of the gap.
"Iris."
That was all, at first. Just her name.
It was a man's voice. Quite low. Quite quiet. He did not raise it at all, but it carried down the whole length of the garden as if he were standing beside her. It was the gentlest voice that Corin had ever heard.
The humming stopped.
It stopped at the top. On the long note. Right in the middle of it, where the tune hung. It did not come down. It just stopped, as if somebody had put a hand flat over it. And the song hung there in the cold still air with nowhere to go, the way a stone hangs at the top of a throw for one moment before it falls.
And it did not fall. It just went. It was not there any more.
"Come in now, my dear," said the gentle voice. "It's growing cold. You'll lose your fingers."
The woman in gray looked up from the bed.
Her calm face turned toward the door, toward the voice. It did not change. It was just as calm as it had been all afternoon. All the way down, with nothing under the water. But she smiled. A small smile, polite and pleasant. The way a woman smiles at a friend of her husband's whose name she cannot quite remember.
"Yes," she said.
She put the trowel down. She did not put it in the basket. She pushed it into the black earth of the bed, point first, so that it stood up out of the ground by itself, the pale wooden handle sticking up among the little mounds. And she got up off her gray leather cushion, slowly, the way you get up when you have been kneeling a long time and your knees are stiff. And she brushed the front of her gray apron with her gloved hands, and the pocket full of white sweets rattled softly. And she picked up the flat basket of bulbs, and held it in front of her in both hands, and walked along the gravel path toward the door.
She left the cushion where it was. She left the trowel standing in the earth.
She walked past the little tin watering can with the daisies painted on it, by the bench, and did not look at it.
"There," said the gentle voice, as she came near. "There. You've planted enough for one day."
The gloved hand let go of the edge of the door, and came out through the gap, and took her hand. The pale gray glove and the dark gray one. And held it. And drew her in, gently, through the door, into the warm, and the light.
And the door closed.
Corin saw the tall shape through the misted glass for a moment longer, and the smaller shape beside it, gray on gray. Then they turned away from the door, together, and went further into the room, and the light took them.
The garden was empty.
The gravel. The hedges. The frozen pool, with the stone fish standing on its tail in the middle of it, with ice in its mouth. The beds with their rows and rows of little mounds. The cushion on the path. The trowel standing up in the earth.
Corin looked down.
His hands were shaking.
He had not noticed it start. He did not know when it had started. He looked down and there they were, both of them, round the cold black iron bars of the railing, black with Abner's coal dust, and they were shaking. Not a little. Not the small shake of cold, or tiredness, or a man who has climbed forty-four steps on one leg. A big shake. A deep one. As if something inside the hands were trying to get out. The iron bars hummed under them. He could hear it. A thin high faint ringing note, going along the railing, from bar to bar.
He told them to stop.
They did not stop.
He took them off the railing and held them in front of him and looked at them, and they shook in the air in front of his face, black and stiff and strange, the coal dust on them showing little pale cracks at the knuckles where the gray came through. He pressed them together. He pressed them flat, palm to palm, the way children are taught to pray. They shook together. He pressed them against his chest, inside the leather cape, against his coat, against his heart, and held them there as hard as he could, and they shook against his heart like two birds in a sack.
He did not know why.
That was what frightened him. Not the shaking. He had shaken before. He had shaken after the wet door, and in the fever, and on the kitchen stair at the Bourse when his knee went. He knew what that was. That was the body, being tired, being hurt. This was not the body. This was something else. This was the hands themselves. As if the hands knew something that he did not. As if they had heard that gentle voice before, a long time ago, somewhere that Corin could not remember, and had never forgotten it, and were trying to tell him.
Who was that? he thought.
Nothing answered.
Who was that?
He thought of the gray seal on the notice. The one that could not be read. Seen. Approved. He thought of Remy in the arches, with his scarred thumbs. Everyone on the Hill knows who wears that ring. They can't remember that they know. He thought of his own account at the Ministry, sealed. Sealed with a seal he had never seen.
And then he stopped thinking about any of it, because it did not fit. It did not fit at all. That voice. You'll lose your fingers. It had been so gentle. It had been the gentlest voice he had ever heard. A man who spoke to his wife like that, at the end of a winter afternoon, calling her in from the cold. That was all it was. A kind man. A careful, kind man, and a woman who could not remember things, and a garden.
His hands shook against his heart.
And inside him, in the dark room behind the door, the held breath let go.
Not all at once. Slowly. The way a man lets out his breath when the footsteps have gone past his hiding place, and down the stairs, and away. And then, very faint, so faint that it was hardly more than the shape of a word, the way the woman's words on the long note had been hardly more than shapes, Malakor spoke.
For the first time in six days.
Go.
Corin stood very still.
Malakor—
Go. A little stronger. Dry and old and sharp, the way it had always been. But there was something in it now that Corin had never heard there before, in all the years he had carried that voice in the back of his head. Not anger. Not impatience. Something much worse than either. Go now, boy. Down. Now. Before he looks out of the window.
Who?
But Malakor did not answer that.
Malakor had gone still again. Not silent. Still. Pressed back against the wall in the dark.
Corin took his shaking hands away from his chest. He took hold of the crutch. He made his fingers close round it, one by one, and they would hardly do it, and he had to look at them to be sure they had hold. And he turned round on the little landing, at the forty-fourth step, with his back to the railings and the garden and the glass doors, and the trowel standing up in the black earth.
And he heard, from above him, from the top of the stair, round the next turn, footsteps coming down.
Quick light even footsteps. And a voice with them, soft and precise, counting.
"Sixty-one. Sixty. Fifty-nine."
